questions.question: Which statement best captures the core idea behind the Cooley–Tukey FFT algorithm for the DFT?
questions.choice_A: It factorizes the dense DFT matrix into a product of sparse, structured factors that can be applied in stages.
questions.choice_B: It approximates the DFT by truncating high-frequency components to reduce computation.
questions.choice_C: It replaces complex multiplications with only additions using quantization.
questions.choice_D: It uses parallel hardware to compute all DFT coefficients independently.

questions.question: In the radix-2 Cooley–Tukey decomposition for an $n$-point DFT with $n=2^m$, how is the problem size reduced at each recursion level?
questions.choice_A: By computing $n/3$ DFTs of size 3 in parallel.
questions.choice_B: By splitting the input into even and odd-indexed samples to form two $n/2$-point DFTs.
questions.choice_C: By downsampling by 2 in the frequency domain.
questions.choice_D: By zero-padding the input and then pruning redundant outputs.

questions.question: What is a primary reason the butterfly graph yields an $O(n \log n)$ algorithm for the DFT?
questions.choice_A: It eliminates all complex multiplications.
questions.choice_B: It compresses the DFT matrix to low rank globally.
questions.choice_C: It exploits a hierarchical sparsity pattern where each stage performs $O(n)$ work over $O(\log n)$ stages.
questions.choice_D: It converts the DFT into a set of independent scalar recurrences.

questions.question: In a radix-2 butterfly, what role do the twiddle factors play?
questions.choice_A: They permute the input indices to bit-reversed order.
questions.choice_B: They normalize the output to ensure unitary scaling.
questions.choice_C: They cancel imaginary components to produce real-valued outputs.
questions.choice_D: They modulate the odd-index DFT subproblem before combination, aligning phases correctly.

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct statement about the DFT of length $n$?
questions.choice_A: It can be written as $X_k = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} x_j \omega_n^{jk}$ where $\omega_n = e^{-2\pi i / n}.$
questions.choice_B: It is defined only for real-valued sequences.
questions.choice_C: It always yields real outputs when the input is complex.
questions.choice_D: It is independent of the choice of the primitive root of unity.

questions.question: Which data movement operation is commonly associated with preparing inputs for in-place radix-2 FFT algorithms?
questions.choice_A: Cyclic shifts by stage-dependent offsets.
questions.choice_B: Bit-reversal permutation of the indices.
questions.choice_C: Random shuffling to improve cache locality.
questions.choice_D: Sorting by magnitude prior to processing.

questions.question: How is a single butterfly operation typically represented in matrix terms?
questions.choice_A: As a dense $n\times n$ matrix multiplying the entire vector.
questions.choice_B: As a diagonal matrix with twiddle factors only.
questions.choice_C: As a product of a sparse $2\times 2$ mixing matrix and a diagonal twiddle factor applied to a pair of elements.
questions.choice_D: As a Toeplitz matrix acting on all even-indexed entries.

questions.question: Which statement about the stage-wise structure of a radix-2 FFT is correct?
questions.choice_A: The first stage uses the largest twiddle exponents and subsequent stages use smaller ones.
questions.choice_B: Every stage mixes all $n$ elements with every other element.
questions.choice_C: There are $\sqrt{n}$ stages, each with $\sqrt{n}$ butterflies.
questions.choice_D: Each stage performs disjoint $2$-point butterflies across the array with increasing stride.

questions.question: Which fast transform also admits a butterfly-like factorization while operating on real-even inputs to avoid complex arithmetic?
questions.choice_A: Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT).
questions.choice_B: Z-transform.
questions.choice_C: Hilbert transform.
questions.choice_D: Short-time Fourier transform (STFT).

questions.question: In terms of computational complexity, why is the FFT preferred over direct DFT evaluation for large $n$?
questions.choice_A: FFT is $O(\sqrt{n})$ while DFT is $O(n)$.
questions.choice_B: FFT is $O(n \log n)$ while DFT is $O(n^2)$, giving substantial savings for large $n$.
questions.choice_C: FFT is exact while DFT is approximate.
questions.choice_D: FFT is GPU-only while DFT is CPU-only.

questions.question: What does the term 'butterfly' specifically refer to in FFT literature?
questions.choice_A: The global algorithmic pattern across all stages.
questions.choice_B: A load-balancing scheme for parallel architectures.
questions.choice_C: The local two-point computation pattern that combines and splits data with twiddle multiplication and sums/differences.
questions.choice_D: A cache prefetching strategy for in-place memory access.

questions.question: Which property of the DFT is directly exploited by the Cooley–Tukey decomposition?
questions.choice_A: Nonlinearity of phase for composite lengths.
questions.choice_B: Time-domain differentiation corresponds to frequency-domain multiplication.
questions.choice_C: Circular convolution theorem only for prime lengths.
questions.choice_D: Periodicity and factorability of roots of unity for composite $n$.

questions.question: What is a key difference between radix-2 decimation-in-time (DIT) and decimation-in-frequency (DIF) FFT variants?
questions.choice_A: DIT splits input into even/odd time indices; DIF splits output into even/odd frequency indices, affecting where twiddles are applied.
questions.choice_B: DIT is in-place while DIF is not.
questions.choice_C: DIT has $O(n^2)$ complexity while DIF has $O(n \log n)$.
questions.choice_D: DIT requires bit-reversal while DIF never does.

questions.question: Which statement about the Hadamard transform in relation to butterfly structures is accurate?
questions.choice_A: It uses additions and subtractions only, with butterflies lacking twiddle factors.
questions.choice_B: It requires complex exponentials as twiddles.
questions.choice_C: It cannot be factored into sparse stages.
questions.choice_D: Its complexity is $O(n^2)$ for $n=2^m$.

questions.question: In matrix-factorization terms, how can an $n$-point radix-2 FFT be viewed?
questions.choice_A: As a single banded matrix of bandwidth 2.
questions.choice_B: As a Vandermonde matrix with a diagonal preconditioner.
questions.choice_C: As a product of $\log_2 n$ sparse block-diagonal matrices interleaved with permutations and diagonal twiddle matrices.
questions.choice_D: As a sum of Kronecker products of identity matrices only.

questions.question: Which practical consideration most directly improves cache locality in in-place FFT implementations?
questions.choice_A: Using higher precision floating-point arithmetic.
questions.choice_B: Replacing butterflies with direct $n$-point DFTs for small $n$.
questions.choice_C: Scheduling computations to operate on contiguous blocks (e.g., iterative, breadth-first stage ordering or cache-oblivious layouts).
questions.choice_D: Avoiding permutations entirely.

questions.question: What is the principal difference between DCT and DST families with respect to boundary conditions?
questions.choice_A: DCT enforces even symmetry at the boundaries, while DST enforces odd symmetry.
questions.choice_B: DCT is non-orthogonal, while DST is orthogonal.
questions.choice_C: DCT requires complex inputs, while DST requires real inputs only.
questions.choice_D: DCT has $O(n^2)$ complexity, while DST has $O(n \log n)$ complexity.

questions.question: Why are bit-reversal permutations often required in radix-2 FFTs?
questions.choice_A: They convert convolution into multiplication.
questions.choice_B: They align data so that the sequence of local butterflies computes the correct global ordering of either inputs or outputs.
questions.choice_C: They reduce numerical roundoff error by shuffling magnitudes.
questions.choice_D: They avoid the need for twiddle factors.

questions.question: Which statement about numerical accuracy in FFT implementations is most appropriate?
questions.choice_A: FFT is immune to floating-point roundoff due to orthogonality.
questions.choice_B: Scaling and twiddle reuse can reduce error growth, but careful ordering and pairwise summation may still be needed for high accuracy.
questions.choice_C: Single precision always suffices because errors cancel out.
questions.choice_D: Iterative refinement is mandatory for all FFT sizes.

questions.question: Which property enables using mixed-radix Cooley–Tukey algorithms for composite lengths $n=ab$?
questions.choice_A: The DFT matrix for length $n$ is block-diagonal for any factorization.
questions.choice_B: Roots of unity satisfy $\omega_n^{ak} = \omega_b^k$ and $\omega_n^{bj} = \omega_a^j$, allowing decomposition into size-$a$ and size-$b$ subtransforms with twiddle factors.
questions.choice_C: The DFT is linear only when $a=b$.
questions.choice_D: Twiddle factors are unnecessary when $a$ and $b$ are coprime.
